Age
 differences
 in
 spatial
 working
 memory
 contributions
 to
 visuomotor
adaptation
Throughout
 our life span we encounter
 challenges
 that require
 us to adapt to the demands
 of our
 chang-
ing
 environment;
 this entails
 learning
 new skills.
 Two primary
 components
 of motor skill learning
 are
motor
 acquisition,
 the initial
 process
 of learning
 the skill, and motor
 transfer,
 when
 learning
 a new skill
 is
beneﬁtted
 by the overlap with a previously
 learned
 one. Older
 adults typically exhibit
 declines
 in motor
acquisition
 compared
 to young
 adults,
 but remarkably,
 do not demonstrate
 deﬁcits
 in motor
 transfer
 [10].
Our
 recent
 work
 demonstrates
 that a failure to engage
 spatial
 working
 memory
 (SWM)
 is associated
 with
skill
 learning
 deﬁcits
 in older adults
 [16]. Here,
 we investigate
 the role that SWM
 plays
 in both motor
learning
 and transfer
 in young
 and older adults.
 Both age groups
 exhibited
 performance
 savings,
 or posi-
tive
 transfer, at transfer
 of learning
 for some
 performance
 variables.
 Measures
 of spatial
 working
 memory
performance
 and reaction
 time correlated
 with both
 motor
 learning
 and transfer
 for young adults. Young
adults
 recruited
 overlapping
 brain
 regions
 in prefrontal,
 premotor,
 parietal
 and
 occipital
 cortex
 for
 per-
formance
 of a SWM and a visuomotor
 adaptation
 task, most notably
 during motor
 learning,
 replicating
our
 prior ﬁndings
 [12]. Neural overlap
 between
 the SWM task and visuomotor
 adaptation
 for the older
adults
 was limited
 to parietal
 cortex, with minimal
 changes
 from
 motor
 learning
 to
 transfer.
 Combined,
these
 results
 suggest
 that age differences
 in engagement
 of cognitive
 strategies
 have a differential
 impact
on
Research
 report
 and
 transfer

Keywords:
Spatial
 working
 memory
Aging
Visuomotor
 adaptation
Skill
 acquisition
Transfer
 motor
 learning
 and transfer.
1.
 Introduction
The
 ability
 to
 adapt
 to
 changes
 in
 the
 world
 around
 us
 is
 an
essential
 life
 skill.
 Learning
 a
 new
 skill
 (“motor
 learning”)
 and
modifying
 it
 to
 meet
 new
 task
 demands
 (“motor
 transfer”)
 are
both
 important
 for
 adaptive
 motor
 behavior
 (reviewed
 in
 ref.
 [1])
at
 all
 stages
 of
 life.
 A
 large
 number
 of
 studies
 have
 documented
age-related
 reductions
 in
 the
 rate
 and
 magnitude
 of
 motor
 skill
acquisition
 (cf.
 [2–7]).
 One
 form
 of
 motor
 learning
 that
 has
 been
widely
 studied
 is
 sensorimotor
 adaptation,
 in
 which
 the
 learner
modiﬁes
 their
 movements
 to
 adjust
 to
 changes
 in
 either
 sensory
input
 or
 motor
 output
 characteristics.
 A
 real-world
 example
 is
learning
 to
 drive
 a
 new
 car;
 the
 magnitude
 of
 vehicle
 movement
 in
response
 to
 the
 amount
 of
 wheel
 turn
 and
 accelerator
 depression
Abbreviations:
 SWM,
 spatial
 working
 memory;
 RT,
 reaction
 time;
 DE,
 directional
error;
 IEE,
 initial
 endpoint
 error.

varies
 across
 vehicles.
 Thus,
 the
 driver
 must
 learn
 the
 new
 mapping
between
 his
 or
 her
 actions
 and
 the
 resulting
 vehicle
 movements.
Both
 young
 and
 older
 adults
 demonstrate
 positive
 motor
transfer
 of
 sensorimotor
 adaptation
 [8–10].
 That
 is,
 prior
 experi-
ence
 with
 one
 form
 of
 adaptation
 results
 in
 better
 performance
of
 another,
 regardless
 of
 age.
 Given
 this
 age
 dissociation,
 with
older
 adults
 exhibiting
 impairments
 in
 initial
 motor
 learning
 but
preserved
 motor
 transfer,
 the
 underlying
 neural
 and
 cognitive
 pro-
cesses
 of
 motor
 learning
 and
 transfer
 may
 be
 distinct
 [11].
We have
 recently
 investigated
 the
 mechanisms
 underlying
 age
impairments
 in
 sensorimotor
 adaptation.
 We administered
 a
 bat-
tery
 of
 neuropsychological
 assessments
 to
 both
 young
 and
 older
adults.
 In
 addition,
 participants
 performed
 a
 manual
 sensorimotor
adaptation
 task
 and
 a
 spatial
 working
 memory
 (SWM)
 task
 while
functional
 magnetic
 resonance
 images
 were
 acquired.
 We found
that
 performance
 on
 the
 card
 rotation
 task,
 a
 measure
 of
 SWM,
 was
correlated
 with
 the
 rate
 of
 early,
 but
 not
 late,
 learning
 of
 a
 visuo-
motor
 adaptation
 task
 for
 young
 adults
 (18
 participants,
 mean
 age
21.1
 ±
 2.5
 years
 [12]).
 There
 were
 no
 correlations
 between
 verbal
working
 memory
 measures
 and
 either
 early
 or
 late
 learning.
 More-
over,
 the
 neural
 correlates
 of
 early
 learning
 overlapped
 with
 those
that
 participants
 engaged
 when
 performing
 a
 SWM
 task,
 notably
 in
